title: Matthew 21:28–32
context: Still answering the temple leaders, Jesus tells the parable of the two sons: one refuses then goes; the other agrees then stays away. Saying yes is not the same as doing the Father’s will—and surprising repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of those who refused John’s light.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 21:28–32, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He answered, I go, sir: but went not - Just so did the scribes and Pharisees: they professed the greatest readiness and zeal in the service of God: but it was bare profession, contradicted by all their actions. John came in a way of righteousness - Walking in it, as well as teaching it.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 21:28–32)

reformed.quote: This conclusion shows what is the object of the parable, when Christ prefers to the scribes and priests those who were generally accounted infamous and held in detestation; for he unmasks those hypocrites, that they may no longer boast of being the ministers of God, or hold out a pretended zeal for godliness. Though their ambition, and pride, and cruelty, and avarice, were known to all, yet they wished to be reckoned quite different persons.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 21:28–32)

verses.text: But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first, and said, ‘Son, go work today in my vineyard.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus opens with a question: What do you think? A father sends the first son to work in the vineyard today. The summons is clear, personal, and urgent—obedience is asked now, not in theory.

Classical Arminians hear enabling grace in the call itself. The Father’s word reaches both sons with moral weight; they are responsible to answer. The parable will turn on whether that summons produces actual work, not mere words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus presses the leaders with a parable about a father’s command: go work in the vineyard today. Authority is paternal and immediate; the vineyard is God’s field of obedience.

Reformed readers hear the King’s authority still in view after the John-question. Providence places this story before hardened shepherds so that saying and doing will expose them—God’s purpose advancing through a simple, searching illustration.

verses.text: He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind, and went.
verses.arminianNotes:
The first son says, “I will not,” then afterward changes his mind and goes. Initial refusal is not illusory; so is the later turn. Repentance here is a change of mind that produces obedience.

Classical Arminians linger on that “afterward.” Under grace, a change of mind remains possible—even after a blunt no. Responsible agency is not erased by prior refusal; the son who once refused can still enter the vineyard and do the Father’s will.
verses.reformedNotes:
The first son refuses, then afterward changes his mind and goes. The turn is not mere regret; it issues in actual work. Effectual turning shows itself in obedience, not in a softer tone alone.

God can grant a change of mind where there was open refusal. The parable’s point is fruit—going into the vineyard—by God’s purpose through an effectual repentance that does what the Father asked.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the first son’s turn as true repentance that issues in obedience. Arminians typically emphasize a change of mind still possible under grace after responsible refusal; Reformed readers stress effectual turning—God’s purpose bringing the son from no to actual work in the vineyard.

verses.text: He came to the second, and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I’m going, sir,’ but he didn’t go.
verses.arminianNotes:
The second son receives the same command and answers politely: “I’m going, sir”—yet he does not go. Respectful speech without obedience is empty. Saying yes can be a way of refusing while looking faithful.

Religious agreement differs from doing the Father’s will. Grace has given clear light; responsible unbelief can hide behind pious words. The tragedy is not rudeness but a yes that never becomes work.
verses.reformedNotes:
The other son says, “I’m going, sir,” but does not go. Verbal assent without obedience is exposed as disobedience. Politeness is not righteousness.

Hardness often wears religious manners. Leaders who confess with the lips while refusing the Father’s call illustrate judicial blindness—profession without fruit under God’s searching judgment.

verses.text: Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said to him, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you.
verses.arminianNotes:
They correctly name the first son as the one who did the father’s will. Jesus then applies it sharply: tax collectors and prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you. Surprising faith and repentance outrun religious refusal.

Listen here for both hope and indictment. Grace made a change of mind possible for notorious sinners who responded; the leaders remain responsible for unbelief. Kingdom entry is by faith that obeys—not by pedigree or polite profession.
verses.reformedNotes:
They answer rightly—“the first”—and Jesus turns the blade: tax collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom before you. God’s purpose brings unlikely believers in ahead of self-assured religion.

Kingdom entry is by God’s purpose through faith, not by religious status. The surprising advance of repentant sinners and the leaders’ lag both serve His sovereign design—grace effectual for some, judicial hardness for those who only say “sir.”
verses.keyContrast: Both hear surprising repentant sinners entering ahead of religious leaders. Arminians underline response under grace versus responsible unbelief that keeps saying yes without going; Reformed readers press God’s purpose—kingdom entry through faith for unlikely believers, and judicial hardness for polite non-doers.

verses.text: For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you didn’t believe him; but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. When you saw it, you didn’t even repent afterward, that you might believe him.
verses.arminianNotes:
John came in the way of righteousness; the leaders did not believe him, but tax collectors and prostitutes did. Even after seeing that fruit, they did not afterward change their minds and believe. Prior light from John was clear; refusal remained responsible.

Arminian interpreters press the even when you saw it. An opportunity to change their minds persisted after public evidence of John’s fruit. Grace invited a later turn like the first son’s; they would not. Religious refusal against known light stands accountable.
verses.reformedNotes:
John came in righteousness; leaders refused belief while tax collectors and prostitutes believed. Seeing that response, they still did not afterward change their minds and believe. Prior prophetic light became a witness against hardened hearts.

Judicial hardness of the leaders. God had sent John; some believed by His purpose through faith, and the leaders’ persistent unbelief—despite visible fruit—displays hardness under judgment, not mere lack of information.
verses.keyContrast: Both root the parable in belief or unbelief toward John’s prior light. Arminians highlight a chance to change their minds after seeing repentant sinners believe—opportunity responsibly refused; Reformed readers highlight effectual faith in the unlikely and judicial hardness in leaders who would not afterward believe.
